messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Modelling heterogeneity of variance
parts:
Hi folks,

In the face of data with clear heterogeneity of variance, I tend to handle it by modelling effects of predictors on the log-sd scale, as in:

  data{
    # nY: length of outcome vector
    int nY ;
    # Y: outcome vector
    vector[nY] Y ;
    # nX: number of predictors
    int nX ;
    # X: predictor matrix (should include intercept)
    matrix[nY,nX] X ;
  }
  parameters{
    # coef_mean: coefficients on predictors' influence on mean
    vector[nX] coef_mean ;
    # coef_sd: coefficients on predictors' influence on sd
    vector[nX] coef_sd ;
  }
  model{
    #normal(0,1) priors, assumes outcome & predictors have been scaled
    coef_mean ~ normal(0,1) ;
    coef_sd ~ normal(0,1) ;
    # outcome as normal with mean & sd influenced by predictors
    Y ~ normal( X*coef_mean , exp(x*coef_sd) ) ;
  }

I like this method because it automatically handles the fact that, once all the effects of the predictors are factored in, it yields values for the sd that are guaranteed to be positive.

Does anyone know of any references I can cite when publishing analyses that use this approach? 

Are there other approaches to modelling heterogeneity of variance that I should check out?

Thanks,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modelling heterogeneity of variance
parts:
It's the typical (inverse) link function for a positive-only
regression in a GLM.

I'd encourage you to name your variable log_coef_sd to keep
the scales clear.

In Stan, if the model's as simple as you wrote, you get
the same effect writing

vector<lower=0>[nX] coef_sd;

That just exp-transfroms an unconstrained variable and applies the
jacobian so you can put a distribution on coef_sd directly.

Or you might want to use some kind of GLM as a model for log_coef_sd.

- Bob
